title: Special timing rules for leases, official conveyances, sheriff conveyances, and wills
mainQuestion: How do the Registry Act special timing rules protect certain leases, auction conveyances, sheriff conveyances, and wills against later purchasers or judgment creditors?
studySummary: Section 19 preserves special registration treatment for selected instruments. Short leases with actual possession need not be registered and are not void merely because they are unregistered, while official auction conveyances, sheriff conveyances, and wills receive the same validity against subsequent purchasers or judgment creditors as if registered at an earlier reference time when they are registered within the stated deadline.

objectives.objective: Recall when a short lease need not be registered.
objectives.guidedQuestion: Which leases are exempt from registration under subsection 19(3), and which leases are excluded from that exemption?
objectives.studyAnswer: A lease for a term not exceeding three years need not be registered if actual possession goes along with the lease, and it is not deemed fraudulent and void merely because it is unregistered. That exemption does not apply to a lease for a term greater than three years or to a lease where actual possession does not go along with the lease.

evidence.evidenceText: 19(3)No lease for a term not exceeding three years, where the actual possession goes along with the lease, need be registered, nor shall such lease be deemed fraudulent and void merely by reason of its not being registered; but this subsection does not extend or apply to any lease for a greater term than three years, nor to any lease where the actual possession does not go along with the lease.

objectives.objective: Recall the timing rule for official auction conveyances.
objectives.guidedQuestion: What registration deadline gives an official public-auction conveyance earlier-effect validity?
objectives.studyAnswer: When a person acting in an official capacity executes a conveyance of an interest in lands sold at public auction pursuant to law, the conveyance is valid against a subsequent purchaser or judgment creditor as if registered at the time of sale if it is registered within six months of the day of sale.

evidence.evidenceText: 19(4)Where a person in an official capacity executes a conveyance of an interest in lands sold at public auction, pursuant to law, the conveyance, if registered within six months of the day of such sale, shall, as against any subsequent purchaser or judgment creditor, be as valid as if registered at the time of sale.

objectives.objective: Recall the timing rule for sheriff conveyances under the Enforcement of Money Judgments Act.
objectives.guidedQuestion: How does subsection 19(4.1) treat a sheriff conveyance registered within six months after execution?
objectives.studyAnswer: Without limiting subsection 19(4), a sheriff conveyance of an interest in lands sold by the sheriff under the Enforcement of Money Judgments Act is valid against a subsequent purchaser or judgment creditor as if registered on the day of execution if it is registered within six months after the day it was executed.

evidence.evidenceText: 19(4.1)Without limiting subsection (4), if a sheriff executes a conveyance of an interest in lands sold by the sheriff under the Enforcement of Money Judgments Act, the conveyance, if registered within six months after the day of its execution, shall, as against any subsequent purchaser or judgment creditor, be as valid as if registered on the day of its execution.

objectives.objective: Recall the will registration deadlines and legal effect.
objectives.guidedQuestion: What deadlines make a will valid against later purchasers or judgment creditors as if registered immediately after death?
objectives.studyAnswer: A will has that validity if registered within six months after the testator’s death when the testator died within the Province, or within one year after death when the testator died without the Province.

evidence.evidenceText: 19(5)A will registered within six months after the death of the testator if he died within the Province, or within one year after death if he died without the Province, shall as against subsequent purchasers or judgment creditors be as valid as if it had been registered immediately after the death of the testator.

title: Deed transfer affidavit and registrar forwarding duty
mainQuestion: What affidavit must accompany registration of a deed transferring real property, and what must the registrar do with that affidavit?
studySummary: A deed affecting transfer of real property cannot be registered unless it is accompanied by an affidavit of transfer with the specified consideration, party, property, and prescribed information. The affidavit must be made by the grantee or an authorized representative in the prescribed or equivalent form, and the registrar must forward it to the Executive Director of Assessment rather than record it.

objectives.objective: Recall the affidavit required for registering a real-property transfer deed.
objectives.guidedQuestion: What must accompany a deed affecting the transfer of real property before it may be registered?
objectives.studyAnswer: It must be accompanied by an affidavit of transfer setting out the true and actual consideration for which the property was acquired, the names of the parties, the location and description of the real property, and any other information prescribed by regulation.

evidence.evidenceText: 19(6)No deed affecting the transfer of real property shall be registered unless accompanied by an affidavit of the transfer setting forth the true and actual consideration for which such property was acquired, the names of the parties, the location and description of real property and such other information prescribed by regulation

objectives.objective: Recall who may make the affidavit and what form it must take.
objectives.guidedQuestion: Who may make the deed transfer affidavit, and what form must it use?
objectives.studyAnswer: The affidavit must be made by the grantee, the grantee’s solicitor, or another agent duly authorized for that purpose, and it must be in the form set out in the regulations or to like effect.

evidence.evidenceText: which affidavit shall be made by the grantee, his solicitor or other agent duly authorized in that behalf, and shall be in the form set forth in the regulations or to the like effect.

objectives.objective: Recall the registrar’s duty after receiving the affidavit.
objectives.guidedQuestion: What must the registrar do with the deed transfer affidavit after registration of the deed?
objectives.studyAnswer: The registrar must not record the affidavit, but must forward it to the Executive Director of Assessment under the Assessment Act no later than thirty days after the deed registration date.

evidence.evidenceText: 19(7)The registrar shall not record such affidavit but shall forward the same to the Executive Director of Assessment under the Assessment Act not later than thirty days after the date of registration of the deed.

title: Boundary confirmation application form and plan standards
mainQuestion: What form and plan standards apply to a boundary confirmation application under Regulation 95-166?
studySummary: A boundary confirmation application made under subsection 6(1) or 6(3) of the Act must use Form 1. The required plan of survey must be current and must conform both to the Association of New Brunswick Land Surveyors standards in effect when the application is made and to any other requirements specified by the Registrar General.

objectives.objective: Recall the required form for a boundary confirmation application.
objectives.guidedQuestion: What form must be used for an application to confirm the location of a boundary?
objectives.studyAnswer: An application to confirm the location of a boundary made under subsection 6(1) or 6(3) of the Act must be in Form 1.

evidence.evidenceText: 3(1)An application to confirm the location of a boundary made under subsection 6(1) or (3) of the Act shall be in Form 1.

objectives.objective: Recall the required standard for the plan of survey.
objectives.guidedQuestion: What standards must the plan of survey satisfy for a boundary confirmation application?
objectives.studyAnswer: The plan of survey required under paragraph 7(1)(a) of the Act must be current and conform in every respect to the Association of New Brunswick Land Surveyors standards in effect when the application is made and to any other requirements specified by the Registrar General.

evidence.evidenceText: 3(2)A plan of survey required under paragraph 7(1)(a) of the Act shall be current and shall conform in every respect to

title: Supporting materials for a boundary confirmation application
mainQuestion: What supporting materials must or may accompany a boundary confirmation application under Regulation 95-166?
studySummary: In addition to the required plan of survey, a boundary confirmation application must include materials that document the survey, the boundary evidence, related instruments, ownership interests, obtained consents or waivers, and other information that assists the Registrar General or is requested. Some items are conditional: existing plans are required when they show the boundary, their related notes and reports are included if reasonably available, and an abstract of title is included if requested by the Registrar General.

objectives.objective: Recall the survey materials that accompany the application.
objectives.guidedQuestion: Which survey-related materials must accompany a boundary confirmation application in addition to the plan of survey?
objectives.studyAnswer: The application must include the field notes and a surveyor’s report conforming with subsection 3(4), prepared by the surveyor who signed the plan of survey. It must also include copies of other existing plans of survey on which the boundary is shown, and, if reasonably available to the applicant, the field notes and surveyor’s reports relating to those plans.

title: Surveyor report contents and Registrar General waiver
mainQuestion: What must a boundary confirmation surveyor’s report contain, and what application requirements may the Registrar General waive?
studySummary: The surveyor’s report required by paragraph 3(3)(a) must identify the issue, trace the boundary history, describe the evidence used to establish the boundary location shown on the plan, and explain why other indicated boundary locations were accepted or rejected. Separately, the Registrar General may waive any subsection 3(3) requirement on terms and conditions the Registrar General considers appropriate.

objectives.objective: Recall the issue, history, and evidence contents of the surveyor’s report.
objectives.guidedQuestion: What issue, history, and evidence descriptions must the surveyor’s report contain?
objectives.studyAnswer: The report must contain a description of the issue to be determined, a description of the history of the boundary in question, and a description of the evidence used to establish the boundary location shown on the plan of survey.

title: Underground storage regulation-making powers
mainQuestion: What subjects may the Lieutenant-Governor in Council regulate under the Underground Storage Act?
studySummary: The Lieutenant-Governor in Council may make regulations about the financial requirements imposed by the Act, designated matter for the definition of fluid, application information, the terms, conditions, and forms of licences, leases, and construction permits, work requirements for licence and permit holders, and matters considered advisable and convenient for carrying the Act into effect.

objectives.guidedQuestion: What financial requirements and fluid-definition matter may be prescribed by regulation?
objectives.studyAnswer: Regulations may prescribe the amount of any fee, rental, or security required by the Act, and may designate matter for the purposes of the definition “fluid”.

title: Regulator assistance to the Board
mainQuestion: When may a regulator assist the Energy and Utilities Board, and what information may the Board receive?
studySummary: For section 49.1, regulator means a regulator as defined in the Financial and Consumer Services Commission Act. After a proceeding has commenced from the application of financial and consumer services legislation, the Board may apply for assistance from a regulator that is not already a party; that regulator may assist without becoming a party, and the Board may receive relevant information from the regulator even if it would not be admissible in court.

objectives.objective: Recall the section-specific meaning of regulator.
objectives.guidedQuestion: What does regulator mean for section 49.1 of the Energy and Utilities Board Act?
objectives.studyAnswer: For section 49.1, “regulator” means a regulator as defined in the Financial and Consumer Services Commission Act.

evidence.evidenceText: 49.1(1)For the purposes of this section, “regulator” means a regulator as defined in the Financial and Consumer Services Commission Act.

objectives.objective: Recall when regulator assistance may be provided.
objectives.guidedQuestion: What must have happened before a non-party regulator may assist the Board under subsection 49.1(2)?
objectives.studyAnswer: The Board must apply following the commencement of a proceeding resulting from the application of financial and consumer services legislation, and the regulator must not already be a party to the proceedings.

evidence.evidenceText: 49.1(2)On application of the Board following the commencement of a proceeding resulting from the application of financial and consumer services legislation, a regulator who is not already a party to the proceedings may render assistance to the Board without becoming a party to the proceedings

objectives.objective: Recall what information the Board may receive from the regulator.
objectives.guidedQuestion: What information may the Board receive and accept from an assisting regulator?
objectives.studyAnswer: The Board may receive and accept information from the regulator that it considers relevant, whether or not the information would be admissible in a court of law.

evidence.evidenceText: and the Board may receive and accept information from the regulator that it considers relevant, whether or not the information would be admissible in a court of law.

title: General supervisor health and safety duties
mainQuestion: What general health and safety duties does every supervisor owe under subsection 9.1(1) of the Occupational Health and Safety Act?
studySummary: Every supervisor has general duties to take reasonable precautions for the health and safety of employees under the supervisor’s supervision and direction, to comply personally with the Act, regulations, and applicable orders, to ensure those employees also comply, and to cooperate with established workplace health and safety bodies, representatives, and enforcement personnel.
